headline_insight: Average understanding looks gender-neutral, but the tail does not: 10.4% of female clients rate their understanding of what their insurance covers as "very poor", against 5.6% of male clients — a 4.8 percentage point gap that survives multiple-comparison adjustment (p_adj = 0.00) and is the only statistically significant gender difference in this section.
paragraphs: At the level of headline averages, insurance literacy in the 2026 survey appears strikingly gender-neutral. Some 39.7% of female clients (n=1,518) and 42.8% of male clients (n=586) rate their understanding of what their policy covers as "good", and a further 35.8% and 36.5% respectively rate it "very good" — differences of 3.1 and 0.7 percentage points that are not statistically significant once adjusted. The same pattern holds for the claims process, where 40.5% of women and 39.6% of men report "good" understanding. Read only from the top of the distribution, one would conclude there is no gender gap to manage.

The tail tells a different story. Women are close to twice as likely as men to report "very poor" understanding of their coverage — 10.4% versus 5.6%, a 4.8 point gap that remains significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons and is the single robust gender finding in this section. A parallel gap appears on the claims process, where 11.5% of women versus 7.3% of men report "very poor" understanding; that 4.2 point difference falls just outside conventional significance after adjustment (p_adj = 0.1) and should be read as directional corroboration rather than an independent finding. Together they point to a concentrated pocket of exclusion — roughly one in ten women who are insured but functionally uninformed — that averages and "good/very good" reporting completely obscure. No external benchmark data was supplied for these understanding indicators, so we cannot situate the size of this gap against peer portfolios or industry norms; we can only observe it within our own client base.

The channel data explains both why understanding is broadly reasonable and why the tail persists. Insurance knowledge in this portfolio travels almost entirely through people, not paper or pixels: 59.4% of women and 60.9% of men name in-person explanation from MFI staff or a loan officer as an effective channel, and 56.4% and 56.7% respectively name group meetings. Everything else is marginal — SMS/WhatsApp (11.9% female, 14.8% male), phone calls (13.1%, 14.0%), printed materials (2.1%, 4.1%) and email (0.4%, 0.2%). The small "other" responses, though far too few (25 clients in total) to be treated as anything but illustrative, are revealing about how information actually flows: clients in Uganda repeatedly named their group leadership rather than the institution, with one female client in Uganda simply answering "The group chairperson" and a male client in Uganda pointing to "some group members". Where the intermediary is a peer rather than a trained officer, message fidelity is unverified — a plausible mechanism behind the very-poor tail, and one this survey can suggest but not prove.

For clients in households with a person with disability (n=477), the survey finds no statistically significant differences from other households on either indicator. "Very poor" understanding of coverage sits at 8.8% versus 9.0%, and "very good" at 36.5% versus 35.9%. The one gap worth watching is "good" understanding of the claims process, at 37.1% for PWD households versus 41.1% for others — a 4.0 point difference that is not significant after adjustment (p_adj = 0.5) and should be treated as directional only, particularly since the section carries no disability-disaggregated data on communication channels at all. That absence is itself a programming finding: we know that insurance understanding is delivered face-to-face and in groups, and we do not know whether those two channels are accessible to clients with mobility, hearing or visual impairments. The implication for product design is twofold. First, remedial effort should be targeted at the bottom decile rather than spread evenly across the portfolio — a short, verbal comprehension check at enrolment and first renewal, with a mandatory re-explanation trigger, would reach the women in the very-poor category that satisfaction-style averages never surface. Second, because group meetings and chairpersons are doing so much of the explanatory work, VisionFund should treat group leaders as a formal training cohort with standardised scripts, and should add disability-disaggregated channel questions to the next survey round so that accessibility of the in-person model can be evidenced rather than assumed. General industry framing on women's financial literacy would predict a gap of this kind, but that is context, not a finding from this survey.
